doc.title: John Altman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 14, 2023

title: Playing with the original Comets: Rock Around the Clock as western swing
summary: He played with the Comets at the Blackboard Jungle anniversary and says their repertoire was swing, compared to Lindy hop and R&B.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: I was going to say, that ages you. That’s fascinating stuff. Just a couple more things here. You had made a statement I believe you were taking about the song “Rock Around the Clock” that there was very little teenage music before that. I’m fascinated by that transition from what we’ll call swing into rock and it’s always struck me that “Rock Around the Clock” is actually a swing tune.

Oh totally. And I got to — which, I think I probably mentioned or you might know, when they had 50 years of “Blackboard Jungle” I got to play with the original Comets so it’s basically everybody who was on the original record apart from Bill Haley and my friend Billy Gusack who played drums because they reckoned that the drummer, Dick, sped up, so they wanted someone to keep the tempo. Anyway so it was basically the original band that toured with Bill Haley. And they played “Shake, Rattle & Roll,” Franny Beecher was there, a great jazz guitarist, Joey Ambrose, the great jazz tenor player, Marshall Little, you know they were all swing musicians, western swing. And they swung like crazy. I mean I got to play on two or three numbers but their basic repertoire was “Rock Around

the Clock” and “Shake, Rattle & Roll” and all these things, were western swing. Absolutely. And the whole rhythmic feel was totally different to that sort of [scats] rock & roll thing that everybody thought straight eighths. It was swing. And it was so infectious, it was incredible. And you could say yeah, this is why they succeeded you know. It was in that tradition. It was swing.
Yeah, so when you watch videos of people doing the Lindy hop at the Savoy there’s really not that much difference from what Bill Haley’s that swing, western swing feel was happening.

Absolutely. I agree. And that’s — I particularly noticed it when they played “Shake, Rattle & Roll” because you get your perception of what it sounded like with Joe Turner and then what it sounded like later. And this was down another path. This really was western swing which of course Joe Turner wasn’t. Joe was R&B and the western swing feel is different from the R&B feel. So it was very interesting to get that and to play with it. Marvelous.
